text: have shown benefit in refractory disease, and some sug- gest zoledronate should be a first-line option.7 Bisphosphonates have superseded calcitonins,1,3,5,6,8 which have a short-lived effect and which generally are less effective in suppressing bone turnover and improving bone pain.2 Calcitonins may still have a role in those pa- tients for whom bisphosphonates are intolerable or inef- fective;5,6 however, resistance to both bisphosphonates and calcitonins may occur.1,4 Plicamycin, a cytotoxic antibiotic with particular activity against osteoclasts, is highly effective in the treatment of Paget’s disease of bone.8 However, it is associated with se- vere toxicity and is therefore now avoided or reserved for patients refractory to other drugs.4,6,8 Studies with gallium nitrate, another inhibitor of bone re- sorption, have indicated beneficial effects in the treatment of Paget’s disease of bone, but long-term haematological safety has not been established,1,8 and routine use is not recommended.6 Ipriflavone has also been reported to be of benefit, but remains investigational for Paget’s disease.8 In selected patients, orthopaedic surgery for a fracture, knee or hip replacement, spinal stenosis, or correction of a bone deformity may be appropriate.4,6,8 A calcitonin or bis- phosphonate may be given for up to 3 months before sur- gery in order to reduce bone vascularity and minimise blood loss during the operation,2,4,8 although this effect has not been verified in studies.6 Such treatment also helps to prevent development of hypercalcaemia due to prolonged immobilisation.4 1.
